comparability.reason: This study provides batch equilibrium isotherm data and qualitative assessments of how source water characteristics affect PFAS adsorption to GAC, but it does not report column, pilot, or full-scale breakthrough, bed volumes, or media lifetime. Batch conditions, ground GAC, and the absence of flow and bed-structure information mean that the results are useful for qualitative comparison and for informing models, but they are not directly comparable on a quantitative basis with continuous-treatment performance metrics.

endpoints.interpretation: Equilibrium batch isotherm tests quantified PFAS uptake by GAC as a function of equilibrium PFAS concentration, to derive adsorption capacities and isotherm parameters and to assess how source water characteristics (NOM, competing PFAS, ions, pH) affect capacity. These measurements address sorption behavior rather than column breakthrough or destruction.
endpoints.reported_term: adsorption capacity; isotherm parameters; PFAS adsorption effectiveness

endpoints.interpretation: While the study discusses GAC “treatment efficacy,” the actual experiments measured equilibrium adsorption capacities and removal in batch, not continuous-treatment breakthrough; removal is therefore interpreted as batch-phase PFAS concentration decrease at equilibrium, conditional on the isotherm tests.
endpoints.reported_term: PFAS removal efficacy; GAC treatment efficacy

endpoints.interpretation: The study evaluates the suitability and limitations of applying ideal adsorbed solution theory (IAST) and AdDesignS-type models for predicting PFAS mixture adsorption from batch isotherm data, highlighting that PFAS trace-level behavior and competition can lead to modeling inaccuracies when scaling to column performance.
endpoints.reported_term: modeling performance of IAST and column-scale design assumptions

limitations.statement: Isotherm (batch) tests do not directly evaluate adsorption breakthrough in GAC columns; modeling tools (e.g., Adsorption Design Software) are required to relate isotherm parameters to full- or pilot-scale breakthrough performance.

Isotherm parameters obtained with ground GAC may need adjustment when used to design or model full- or pilot-scale GAC systems with larger particle sizes, due to particle-size impacts on adsorption behavior and kinetics.

Ideal adsorbed solution theory (IAST) performed poorly for PFAS mixtures, with and without NOM, and may be insensitive when modeling trace constituents like PFAS; using IAST as currently implemented can therefore lead to errors in predicting GAC performance from batch data.

limitations.statement: The forward-modeling approach provides useful qualitative insight into PFAS breakthrough behavior, but the authors recommend that pilot-scale column verification experiments be conducted when sufficient water quantities are available.

endpoints.interpretation: Batch tests with BIPGEM showed high removal efficiencies for long-chain PFAS (PFOA, PFOS) in a PFAS mixture, while dynamic column tests quantified time-dependent removal and breakthrough behavior, with better performance for long-chain PFAS than for short-chain PFAS.

endpoints.interpretation: Breakthrough curves for short-chain PFAS (e.g., PFBA, PFBS) were steeper and exhibited earlier breakthrough than long-chain PFAS, reflecting stronger competitive adsorption and preferential uptake of PFOA and PFOS by BIPGEM.
endpoints.reported_term: dynamic removal efficiency and breakthrough curves

limitations.statement: Dynamic fixed-bed column tests were conducted at bench scale with a single specialty media (BIPGEM) and a specific PFAS mixture in C-23 canal water, limiting direct translation of removal efficiencies and breakthrough behavior to other adsorbents, water matrices, and full-scale systems.

While Thomas, Yoon–Nelson, and MDR models were applied to fit breakthrough curves, the excerpts do not report fitted parameter values, breakthrough criteria (e.g., C/C0 threshold), or bed volumes treated, which constrains quantitative scale-up analysis.

comparability.reason: Bench-scale AE column operated in continuous flow with defined EBCT, bed volume, PFAS-spiked finished drinking water, and a consistent breakthrough definition (C/C0 = 0.1), producing removal vs. bed volume data that are structurally comparable to other fixed-bed adsorption systems when adjusted for EBCT and influent concentrations.

endpoints.interpretation: PFAS removal assessed from effluent concentrations over time; breakthrough defined at C/C0 = 0.1 and expressed as bed volumes treated and time to breakthrough; model-derived half-saturation time (t) also used to characterize capacity and kinetics
endpoints.reported_term: removal efficiency and breakthrough bed volumes

endpoints.interpretation: Model parameter t used to describe time to half saturation of AE column for co-removal of 14 PFASs; longer t in Phase 2 interpreted as increased effective capacity potentially due to PFAS agglomeration on DOC-loaded media
endpoints.reported_term: half-saturation time (t) from Lin and Huang column model

limitations.statement: Column behavior exhibited two phases, with Phase 2 showing greater apparent removal capacity, likely related to PFAS agglomeration on DOC-loaded media; authors note that Phase 2 parameters may be more relevant for predicting DWTP performance.

The Lin and Huang model fit AE results better than GAC results (R2 = 0.92) but still showed compound-specific deviations, particularly for PFOA, indicating uncertainty in predictive capacity across PFAS.

Adsorption mechanisms and the role of PFAS aggregation on AE surfaces could not be conclusively determined; authors call for further surface-structure analyses (e.g., SEM) to verify agglomeration or micelle/hemi-micelle formation.
Bench-scale columns used one finished drinking water source and a fixed influent PFAS concentration, so scale-up to variable full-scale conditions and other source waters may be uncertain.

comparability.reason: Bench-scale GAC column operated in continuous flow with defined EBCT, bed volume, PFAS-spiked finished drinking water, and common breakthrough definition (C/C0 = 0.1), enabling comparison with other fixed-bed adsorption studies provided differences in EBCT, influent quality, and PFAS mixture are considered.

endpoints.interpretation: PFAS removal assessed from effluent concentrations over time; breakthrough defined at C/C0 = 0.1 and expressed as bed volumes treated; attention to variation in breakthrough BVs by PFAS chain length and functional group.
endpoints.reported_term: removal efficiency and breakthrough bed volumes

limitations.statement: Removal efficiencies in the GAC column decreased from startup to final sampling for all PFASs except PFTeDA and PFDoDA, indicating limited capacity and complex loading effects that challenge simple extrapolation of early-time performance to media lifetime.
Breakthrough bed volumes and removal behavior varied substantially by PFAS chain length and functional group, so a single design safety factor cannot uniformly predict breakthrough for all PFASs.

Bench-scale GAC column used one PFAS mixture and one drinking water source; real full-scale systems may experience different competitive adsorption from varying DOC and co-contaminants, limiting direct scale-up.
